caption: Self-portrait under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A person and a car stand in the Atacama desert beneath a sky crowded with stars, and both throw a shadow onto the ground. The figure is ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek, and the light casting that shadow does not come from the Moon or a lamp. It comes from the bright band of the Milky Way itself.

On a clear night with no Moon, the stars of our own galaxy become almost the only source of light for miles around this remote corner of Chile. Under skies that dark, even the black and brown clouds of molecular gas threaded through the Milky Way stand out against the glow of the stars behind them.
Far off on the horizon sit the four Very Large Telescopes on Cerro Paranal. While the photographer worked, they were busy recording objects inside our galaxy and well beyond it.
explore: ESO opens its observatories to thousands of visitors each year. Guests can tour the sites, see the instruments used to photograph the sky, and learn about the work of some of the largest ground-based astronomy facilities anywhere on Earth.

The rising glow is zodiacal light, which is sunlight bouncing off dust that drifts between the planets in the plane of the ecliptic, the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky.

Near the top of the picture, part of the central bulge of our galaxy shows through. The dark lanes along the Milky Way are enormous clouds of interstellar dust that soak up visible light and give the energy back out at longer wavelengths.

story: The Milky Way arches across the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory. The instrument beneath it is the ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope, one of the facilities at this site in northern Chile.

The arch is our own galaxy seen from the inside. We live within a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, so when we look along that disc, the light of countless distant stars merges into a pale band that wraps around the sky.

La Silla sits 2400 metres up, on the fringe of the Atacama Desert, some 600 km from Santiago de Chile to the south. Being so far from city lights gives the observatory one of the darkest night skies on the planet, which helps a band as faint as this stand out above the telescope.
explore: A Schmidt telescope is a design that trades fine detail on a single object for a wide field of view, which makes it well suited to surveying large patches of sky.

The Milky Way appears as a band because the Sun sits inside a flat disc of stars. Looking along the plane of that disc, we see so many distant stars stacked up that their light blends into a single glowing river, interrupted in places by clouds of dust.

The observatory is on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert, about 600 km north of Santiago de Chile, at an altitude of 2400 metres. That remote, high location keeps it far from light pollution, and ESO describes its night sky as one of the darkest on Earth. caption: Star trails over the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars sweep across the night sky in trails above a retired telescope on a Chilean mountaintop. The instrument is the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, known as SEST, at ESO's La Silla Observatory in the Atacama Desert.

Star trails like these come from long or stacked exposures. The stars themselves are not racing across the sky. Earth's rotation carries the camera around, so each point of starlight is drawn out into an arc.

SEST was retired in 2003. It was shut down to make way for two newer facilities, the APEX telescope (Atacama Pathfinder Experiment) and the ALMA array (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array). Even so, the old dish has not been removed. It still stands on its mountain at La Silla, now a quiet foreground for photographs of the turning sky rather than a working instrument.
explore: Submillimetre telescopes collect light at wavelengths longer than infrared but shorter than radio waves, which is useful for studying cold gas and dust. That is why they use dishes rather than the mirrors inside the domes of optical telescopes.

ESO presents the photograph as proof of how clear the night sky is at this site. The summit of Cerro Paranal stands 2600 metres high. That clarity is the reason the Very Large Telescope was built here, as part of the Paranal Observatory.

For any large observatory, the quality of the sky matters a great deal. Clouds and haze get in the way of faint starlight, so a site with unusually clear nights gives telescopes a better chance of recording dim, distant objects. The Milky Way arching over the desert here is the evidence ESO points to.

story: The Milky Way streaks overhead, where glowing gas, dark dust and countless sparkling stars stand out vividly against the blacker sky around them. In the foreground, the entrance to ESO's Paranal Observatory frames the plane of our galaxy.

Paranal is ESO's flagship observatory and one of the best places in the world for looking at the sky. It sits more than 2600 metres above sea level in Chile's Atacama Desert, well away from the light pollution that human settlements produce.

The glowing band is our galaxy seen edge-on from within. Stars, glowing gas and lanes of dust all lie in a flattened disc, and we see that disc as a stripe across the sky. From a site this dark, the contrast between the bright star clouds and the dark dust is easy to capture, which is exactly why astronomers value such locations.

story: The Magellanic Clouds hang in the sky over the Auxiliary Telescopes that belong to ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal, Chile. They are two small galaxies that keep company with our own, and here they share the sky with the telescopes built to study the Universe beyond.
The Magellanic Clouds are dwarf galaxies, far smaller than the Milky Way, and they orbit around its centre as satellites. Each is a separate galaxy with its own stars, gas and dust.

They can only be seen from the Southern Hemisphere, which makes them a familiar sight above Chile's observatories and an unfamiliar one to most skywatchers in the north. As close companions of the Milky Way, they give astronomers a chance to study another galaxy's stars from relatively nearby.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars draw long trails across the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory, while the trail of an aircraft runs over the horizon. The picture combines a series of night exposures taken looking toward the east.

The trails do not mean the stars are moving. They record the sky's apparent motion over the course of a night, which is really Earth spinning on its axis and carrying the camera with it. The celestial south pole lies out of frame, toward the upper right, and the celestial equator runs from the top left corner of the frame down to the horizon.

Several of the observatory's telescopes appear. Front and centre stands the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, and the NTT and the ESO 3.6-metre telescope stand in the background. Off to the right in the distance is SEST, the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope.
explore: Near the celestial pole, star trails bend into tight circles, while near the celestial equator they run as almost straight lines. That is why the curvature of the trails changes across a wide view like this one.

story: A winding road climbs toward Cerro Paranal under a starry sky. Near the top left of the picture shines Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. The road leads up to ESO's Very Large Telescope.

Sirius belongs to the constellation Canis Major, the Greater Dog, where it marks the animal's neck. Other stars of the constellation appear as well. The dog's head lies to the left of Sirius, and three nearly aligned stars to its right trace a hind leg.

Over in the right part of the image is another bright star, Canopus, which belongs to Carina, the Keel. Constellations are patterns that people have drawn among stars that usually lie at very different distances from us, so the shape of the dog is a matter of perspective rather than a physical grouping.

story: A red glow lingers behind the mountains where the Sun sits low, fading upward into a blue-black sky. Above the desert, the Milky Way spreads out richly, its stars appearing in purple tones. Babak Tafreshi photographed this night sky over Chile's Atacama Desert.

The scene captures a moment of overlap between day and night. Sunlight scattered by the atmosphere still colours the horizon, while higher up the sky has already darkened enough for the band of our galaxy to show through, so both kinds of light appear in one photograph.
The Milky Way is our home galaxy seen from inside its flat disc. Its countless distant stars, too faint to pick out one by one, merge into a soft, glowing band that stretches above the desert.
explore: Photographers often work in this brief window between sunset and full darkness, when a sky still holding a trace of colour can be combined with the first stars and the glow of the Milky Way.

story: At La Silla Observatory, the home of ESO's 3.6-metre telescope stands beneath a starry sky crossed by the Milky Way. The telescope is one of the most effective instruments available for finding planets around other stars.

It started work in 1977 and, more than 40 years on, is still producing important results. Regular improvements, including a new secondary mirror, have kept it among the most productive telescopes on the planet. It is also still the biggest telescope at La Silla.

Much of its planet-hunting power comes from HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher. HARPS is a spectrograph, an instrument that splits starlight into its colours. It watches for tiny shifts in a star's light as an unseen planet tugs the star back and forth. ESO says its precision is unmatched and that it holds many records in exoplanet research.
explore: La Silla as a whole is a busy scientific site, and work from the observatory feeds into more than 300 research papers each year.

story: Stars wheel around a single point in the sky above a telescope dome at ESO's La Silla Observatory. On the left, a lighter, hazy patch softens the darkness. The picture was built from a long series of night exposures taken looking south.

The trails reveal the sky's apparent motion, which is really Earth turning on its axis. Every star seems to circle the celestial south pole, which appears here on the right, just above the dome in the foreground. The nearer a star lies to that point, the smaller the circle it traces.

The diffuse glow on the left comes from the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. These are two irregular galaxies that are neighbours of the Milky Way. Each is a galaxy in its own right, lying outside the Milky Way, and from La Silla they appear as a soft, lighter area in the southern sky.
explore: Photographs pointed at the celestial pole are a favourite of night-sky photographers, because the concentric circles show at a glance how the whole sky appears to pivot around one spot as the planet spins.

story: A dry riverbed runs through the foreground while the Milky Way streams across the sky above it. ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took the picture near ESO's Paranal Observatory in the Atacama Desert, which ranks among the driest places on Earth.

The photograph plays on two kinds of river. On the ground, the channel carved by long-gone water is empty. Overhead, the band of our galaxy looks like a flowing stream of light. One has dried up, while the other, as ESO puts it, keeps delivering new discoveries about the cosmos.

That dryness is part of why ESO built here. Dry air generally means clearer skies, which is what sensitive telescopes need. On these arid plains, ESO has designed and built what it describes as the most productive observatory in the world.
explore: The Milky Way appears as a band because we view our galaxy's flat disc from inside it, so the light of many distant stars merges into a continuous glow broken by dark dust.

story: Dotted trails of stars run across the sky above the summit of Cerro Armazones, with an instrument standing on the right. The picture combines multiple exposures taken looking west from the top of this 3046-metre-high mountain, the site chosen for ESO's Extremely Large Telescope.

Because Earth rotates, the night sky appears to turn around the southern celestial pole. When a series of exposures is stacked, each star leaves a line of dots along its path. The gaps between the dots mark the breaks between individual frames.

The shape of the trails depends on where they sit in the sky. Toward the celestial equator, which lies near the left edge of this view, the trails run straighter. The instrument on the right is the Differential Image Motion Monitor, or DIMM. It measures atmospheric seeing, the blurring caused by turbulent air, which is a key test of any site for a giant telescope.
explore: Measuring the seeing before building is essential, because a large mirror cannot deliver sharp images if the air above it constantly shimmers, so instruments like the DIMM help confirm that a mountaintop is worth the investment.

story: Stars trace dotted circles around a point near the centre of this image, taken from the summit of Cerro Armazones. That point is the south celestial pole. The mountain, 3046 metres high, was chosen as the site of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope.

The picture combines multiple exposures. As Earth rotates, the whole night sky appears to turn around the southern celestial pole, and each star moves a little between frames. Stacked together, the frames turn every star into a line of dots curving around the centre.

Two pieces of equipment appear in the frame. The instrument on the right, the Differential Image Motion Monitor or DIMM, measures atmospheric seeing, meaning how much turbulence in the air blurs the view. To its left rises a white and red tower, the meteorological station. Together they gathered the kind of information needed to judge whether the summit would suit a giant telescope.
explore: Stars close to the pole trace small, tight circles, while those farther away sweep out wide arcs, so the pattern of trails is a kind of map of the sky's rotation.

caption: Orion and the Milky Way above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The constellation Orion hangs upside down above ESO's Very Large Telescope, as though diving toward the Atacama Desert. It appears head down because the VLT is in the Southern Hemisphere. Below, the four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes point up at the night sky.

The Milky Way, crossed by dark lanes of dust, rises over Melipal, the third Unit Telescope, and the bright star Capella glints just above it. Up and to the left, Orion's belt and sword, which holds the Orion Nebula, sit between blue Rigel and orange Betelgeuse.

The picture is packed with other sights. The red Rosette Nebula glows in the middle part of the Milky Way, and Sirius, the brightest star of the night sky, hangs over the whole scene. Just above Unit Telescope 2, Kueyen, a red patch marks the California Nebula, with the blue Pleiades star cluster a little to its upper left.
explore: The colours of stars carry information. A blue star such as Rigel is hotter than an orange one such as Betelgeuse. Red nebulae like the Rosette and California glow because of hydrogen gas energised by nearby stars.

It may come as a surprise that a European observatory works in the northern Chilean desert. But the vast Atacama gives astronomers exactly what they need, which is dry air and very clear skies. The qualities that make this landscape look so empty are the ones that draw telescopes to it.
explore: ALMA, the observatory on the nearby Chajnantor plateau, is a large array of antennas that studies the sky at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, well beyond the colours our eyes can see.

story: Stars streak across the sky above the telescopes of ESO's La Silla Observatory in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Farid Char. Their light has been drawn out into long arcs.

story: Stars leave trails across the night sky over Paranal Observatory, visible on the mountain at right. From one of the telescopes, an orange beam of light reaches up into the darkness, and higher in the sky float two elongated, cloud-like shapes.

The orange beam is a laser, used to measure turbulence in the atmosphere. In a single quick snapshot it would be a thin line. Because the camera collected light for so long, the beam has spread out into a wide fan instead.

caption: Cacti beneath the Milky Way near ALMA, Chajnantor, Chile
story: Tall cacti stand beneath the Milky Way, which is on full display across the sky. In the lower right glows the Large Magellanic Cloud. Stéphane Guisard captured this view in the Chilean Atacama Desert.

story: Star trails form an archway over ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory, high in the Chilean desert. The telescopes below stand still while the sky seems to wheel above them.

The VLT is not a single instrument. It is made up of four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes and four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes. Together they share this high desert site, and the photograph gathers all of them under a single sweep of sky.

The arch of trails comes from Earth's rotation. During a long exposure, the camera turns with the planet, and each star traces a curve across the image. Only the sky appears to move, because everything on the ground, including the telescopes, is turning along with the camera. The result compresses a stretch of the night into one frame.
explore: The pattern of star trails changes with the direction the camera faces. Near a celestial pole they curl into circles, while elsewhere they form long arcs like these.

understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points. Only a long exposure can record their apparent motion as arcs.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Star trails hang in the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory. Alexandre Santerne captured it with a long series of exposures taken at night.

The trails come from the apparent motion of the sky. The stars are not moving in the way they seem to be. Earth is turning on its axis, and the observatory and camera turn with it. From the ground, that rotation makes every star appear to travel slowly across the sky.

Each frame freezes the stars in one position. When the frames are combined, those positions join into curved lines, showing in a single image a motion too slow to follow by eye. The technique turns an ordinary starry night into a picture of our planet's spin, with the observatory standing still beneath it.
explore: La Silla is one of ESO's observatory sites in Chile, and its telescopes and dark skies are a frequent subject for ESO's Photo Ambassadors. Alexandre Santerne is one of them.

understand.summary: This is a series of night-time photographs taken in visible light with a camera at La Silla and combined into one image. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points. The trails appear only because many exposures were combined.

caption: Star trails over the VLT platform, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Long star trails run through the sky above the telescope platform at ESO's Paranal Observatory, where the Auxiliary Telescopes stand. The picture was built from a long series of night-time exposures by Babak Tafreshi.

The trails show the apparent motion of the sky. The stars only seem to travel. The real movement belongs to Earth, which spins on its axis and carries the observatory and the camera with it. Through the night, that spin makes every star appear to sweep slowly across the sky.

A single short exposure would catch each star as a dot. Stacking many exposures joins those dots into smooth arcs, turning a whole stretch of the night into one image. The ground turns along with the camera, so only the distant sky records the motion.
explore: The Auxiliary Telescopes are the smaller telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, housed on the same summit platform as the four large Unit Telescopes.

caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The soft glow of the Milky Way stretches across the sky and seems to graze the tops of the enclosures of ESO's Very Large Telescope. The VLT stands at the Paranal Observatory in Chile, a location that ESO says offers some of the most spectacular views of the cosmos.

The band of light is our own galaxy, seen from within. The Sun sits inside a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust. When we look along that disc, the light of a vast number of distant stars blends into a glowing strip, broken up by darker clouds of dust in front of it.

Placing the telescopes against that backdrop connects the instruments with their subject. The VLT's large mirrors are built to gather far more light than any camera lens, so they can study the Milky Way as well as objects far beyond it.
explore: Paranal's dark skies make views like this possible.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers much more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter here than it would to someone standing on the platform.

caption: ALMA antennas under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: A group of 12-metre dish antennas turn toward targets in the night sky, as the Milky Way crosses the picture through a field of countless stars. The antennas belong to the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA, and this is only a part of the array.

ALMA's dishes work very differently from the camera that recorded this scene. They are tuned to light at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, far longer than the visible light our eyes and ordinary cameras detect. By combining signals from many antennas, the array can behave like a single much larger telescope.

Above them, the Milky Way appears as a luminous band, the combined light of countless distant stars in the disc of our galaxy, with darker patches where dust blocks the view. This photograph by A. Duro sets the antennas, turned toward their targets, beside the galaxy stretched above them.
explore: ALMA stands on the Chajnantor plateau in the Chilean Atacama.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at ALMA. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would in person.

caption: The Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds above La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The glow of the Milky Way and the two Magellanic Clouds hangs above a pair of telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. ESO says the skies over this site offer some of the most spectacular views anywhere.

Three galaxies share this sky. The Milky Way is our own, seen from the inside as a band of light formed by countless distant stars. The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are separate, smaller galaxies, dwarf companions of the Milky Way that appear as separate hazy patches.

From the Southern Hemisphere, the Magellanic Clouds are a familiar feature of dark skies. Because they are so close to us, astronomers can study their stars and gas in far more detail than they can in more distant galaxies.
explore: Dark, clear skies like those at La Silla let a camera capture the soft glow of neighbouring galaxies.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at La Silla. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The Magellanic Clouds can be seen with the naked eye under dark skies, but a long exposure shows them, and the Milky Way, brighter than they would appear in person.

alt: The Milky Way and two hazy cloud-like galaxies in the night sky above two telescopes.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Star trails wheel across the sky above a group of telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory. The photograph, credited to F. Char, gathers five of them in one scene.

Beneath the trails sit the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, the ESO New Technology Telescope, known as NTT, the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, plus the smaller ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope. Together they show the variety of instruments that have been built on this mountain over the years, from optical telescopes of different sizes to a dish designed for submillimetre light.

The trails themselves record Earth's rotation. While the camera collected light, the planet turned, and each star was drawn out into a curve across the sky. The telescopes turn along with the camera, so only the distant stars appear to move.
explore: La Silla's telescopes range from the ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope to the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, and the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope works at wavelengths far longer than visible light.

caption: Star trails over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: Stars sweep in circles around a point on the left side of this picture, taken looking south over Chile's Atacama Desert. That point is the celestial south pole. The image was made from a long series of night-time exposures by Babak Tafreshi.

The circles are the result of Earth's rotation. As the planet spins on its axis, the sky appears to turn around the celestial poles, the points directly above Earth's own poles. Stars near the south pole trace tight rings, while stars farther away sweep out wider arcs.

Individually, each exposure shows stars as points. Combined, the frames link those points into trails. Looking south from the Southern Hemisphere, the pattern is centred on the pole, but no bright star marks that spot, so it shows up only as the hub of the circles.
explore: The picture looks south over the Atacama Desert, where, as for anyone in the Southern Hemisphere, the celestial south pole is always above the horizon.

understand.summary: This is a series of night-time photographs taken in visible light with a camera in the Atacama Desert and combined into one image. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points. Only by combining many exposures can a camera show them circling the pole.

caption: The Milky Way rising over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The faint, diffuse glow of the Milky Way, only just visible among a sea of stars, rises from behind distant peaks in Chile's Atacama Desert. In the foreground, a desert road and the plants around it are lit by a weak red lamp.

Red light is often used at night by astronomers and photographers because it disturbs dark-adapted eyes less than white light. It picks out the road and the vegetation without washing out the sky above.

The Milky Way is our own galaxy, seen from inside its disc, where the light of distant stars blends into a soft band. It is just emerging from behind the mountains, so only part of its glow is on show. The photograph is by Carlos A. Durán.
explore: The red lamp in the foreground is described as weak, but it lights the road and plants enough to show them.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera in the Atacama Desert. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way may appear more distinct here than it would in person, though the caption notes it is only just visible.

caption: Star trails around the celestial south pole over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The whole sky seems to pivot around one spot, the celestial south pole, leaving curving star trails behind it. Closer to home, distant orange glows mark where people live around the Chilean Atacama Desert. The photograph is by Carlos A. Durán.

The swirl is an effect of Earth's rotation. Because the planet spins on its axis, the whole sky appears to turn around the celestial poles. Over a long exposure, each star traces an arc around that centre, and the arcs grow larger for stars farther from the pole.

The orange glows tell a different story. They come from towns and settlements, whose lights brighten the sky above them. Even in the Atacama, human light shows up in the picture, and dark skies are easily brightened.
explore: The celestial south pole is the point in the sky directly above Earth's South Pole, and it is only visible from the Southern Hemisphere.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera in the Atacama Desert. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points. Only a long exposure records their motion around the pole as trails.

caption: An ALMA antenna under the Milky Way, Operations Support Facility, Chile
story: A single 12-metre antenna stands alone under the night sky, while the Milky Way stretches across the image amid a sea of stars. This antenna is one of many that make up the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA.

It is not yet in its working place. The dish is waiting at the Operations Support Facility to be transported. ALMA's antennas are designed to be combined, and together they collect light at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which lie well beyond what human eyes can see.

The scene shows a quiet moment in the life of a large observatory, with a lone antenna waiting beneath the night sky. The Milky Way above is our home galaxy seen from within, its glow built from the light of countless distant stars.
explore: An array like ALMA works by combining signals from many antennas, so each individual dish is one part of a much larger instrument. This one is still waiting to join the rest.
