caption: Reaching for Jupiter beneath the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Standing at the head of a staircase, ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek reaches up toward what looks like a single very bright star among many. It is actually the planet Jupiter, shining in front of thousands of stars that belong to the Milky Way.

The Milky Way arcs across this panorama and leads the eye down to the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope. Our galaxy contains billions of stars, and the ones visible here are only a tiny share of them.

At the far left of the photograph are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, the Milky Way's two satellite galaxies. The scene layers distances in one frame, from a nearby planet within our Solar System to stars inside our galaxy and two separate galaxies beyond it, all appearing side by side from where the photographer stands.
explore: Planets such as Jupiter can outshine most stars in the night sky, which is why they are easily mistaken for unusually bright stars. The playful pose makes use of that.

understand.summary: This is a panoramic landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: Jupiter is easy to see with the naked eye, but a long exposure reveals far more stars and makes the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds brighter than they would appear in person.

alt: A person at the top of a staircase reaching toward a bright point of light, with the Milky Way arcing over four large telescopes and two hazy galaxies at far left.

caption: Twilight panorama from Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: This twilight panorama looks south from Cerro Armazones, the mountain chosen for the planned Extremely Large Telescope. Just behind a tall tower rises the Milky Way, and on the right hang the fuzzy Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. ESO Photo Ambassador Serge Brunier made the image.

The Magellanic Clouds are two irregular galaxies that neighbour our own. Unlike the neat spiral or elliptical shapes of many larger galaxies, irregular galaxies have no clear overall structure, and from the Southern Hemisphere these two appear as pale, detached patches of light.

The picture also contains the south celestial pole, a point you cannot see directly, around which the southern stars appear to turn. It lies to the left of the Magellanic Clouds, and together with the two galaxies it forms a roughly equilateral triangle, a handy pattern for finding the pole.
explore: At the time of this photograph, the Extremely Large Telescope was still a plan, and Cerro Armazones had been selected as its future home. The tall tower shows the scale.

understand.summary: This is a panoramic landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at twilight. The camera settings, colour processing and panorama projection are not published.
understand.eye: The Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way are visible to the eye under dark skies, but a camera exposure makes them brighter and clearer than they would appear at twilight.

alt: A twilight panorama of a mountaintop with a tall tower, the Milky Way rising behind it and two fuzzy galaxies on the right.

caption: Night view of La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: This night view shows La Silla Observatory, which ESO calls its first observatory, set on the outskirts of the Chilean Atacama Desert. The photograph was taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition by Babak Tafreshi.

La Silla sits 600km north of Santiago, at the edge of Chile's Atacama Desert. Today many of ESO's Member States use the site for targeted projects, focused programmes that make use of the telescopes on the site rather than general observing.

Observatories are generally built far from city lights, where dark skies give telescopes the best chance of catching faint light. La Silla, as ESO's first observatory, has a long history of watching the southern sky, and this picture is a portrait of that site at night.
explore: The ESO Ultra HD Expedition was a photography project at ESO's sites in Chile, and this view of La Silla is one of its images.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at La Silla. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure collects more light than the eye can, so the night sky appears brighter and richer in stars than it would to a visitor.

alt: A night view of La Silla Observatory.

caption: Lights near and far above Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This night scene from Paranal gathers a wide range of light sources, from very close to extremely distant. Closest of all is a laser shining up into the sky, used to measure turbulence in the atmosphere.

Farther away, on the ground, are the lights of the city of Antofagasta and of the Escondida copper mine. Higher up, the upper atmosphere itself glows green, and at the upper left a white glow comes from dust between the planets reflecting sunlight.

Beyond our Solar System, the picture reaches the Orion Nebula, a cloud of gas in our own galaxy, and the Milky Way itself. Farthest of all is the Large Magellanic Cloud, a separate galaxy neighbouring ours. In one frame, then, the photograph spans a human-made beam, towns and industry, Earth's own air, the Solar System, our galaxy and another galaxy beyond it.
explore: The green glow of the upper atmosphere is known as airglow, faint light given off by atoms and molecules high above the ground, even on the darkest nights.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: Several of these light sources, such as the airglow and the dust glow, are too faint to see clearly by eye, but a camera exposure collects enough light to reveal them.

alt: A night sky with a laser beam, distant city and mine lights, a green glow from the upper atmosphere, a white glow at upper left, the Milky Way and a hazy galaxy.

caption: Barnard's Loop and the Magellanic Clouds over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The plane of the Milky Way arches over the Atacama Desert in northern Chile in this wide panorama by Petr Horálek. Above the band, a half-ring of pink light curves through the sky, and toward the upper right float two pale, diffuse clouds.

The pink arc is Barnard's Loop, a huge, faint shell of glowing gas. It is hard to pick out by eye, but this deep exposure collects enough light to bring it out. Pink and red glows in astronomy photographs usually come from hydrogen gas being energised by nearby stars.

The two pale clouds are the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, neighbouring galaxies of the Milky Way. Together with the arch of our galaxy and the loop of gas, they make this panorama a gathering of sights that only show up well in long exposures from very dark places.
explore: ESO describes this as a deep exposure, which is what lets faint features such as Barnard's Loop show up at all.

understand.summary: This is a deep-exposure panoramic landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera in the Atacama Desert. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: Barnard's Loop is very hard to see with the eye alone, but a deep camera exposure gathers enough of its faint light to show the pink arc.

alt: The Milky Way arching over a desert, with a faint pink half-ring above it and two pale cloud-like galaxies toward the upper right.

caption: The Milky Way, the Moon and Jupiter over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way cuts across the night sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, while off to the right the Moon and Jupiter shine very brightly. Below, a whole suite of telescopes stands on the mountain.
Many of those telescopes are used by ESO's Member States for targeted projects, where teams concentrate on particular scientific questions using the instruments at the site.

The sky shows objects at wildly different distances. The Moon is our closest neighbour, Jupiter is a planet in our own Solar System, and the Milky Way is the combined glow of countless distant stars in our galaxy. Through a camera they share a single frame. The brightness of the Moon and Jupiter also shows why astronomers pay attention to moonlight, since a bright Moon lights up the sky and can make faint objects harder to observe.
explore: The photograph is credited to Babak Tafreshi.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at La Silla. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The Moon and Jupiter are easy to see by eye, but the long exposure makes the Milky Way much brighter than it would appear with the Moon up.

alt: The Milky Way across a night sky above several telescope domes, with the bright Moon and Jupiter on the right.

caption: Centaurus A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view looks into the dusty heart of Centaurus A, also known as NGC 5128, a galaxy famous for its prominent lanes of dark material. The observations were made with Wide Field Camera 3, Hubble's most advanced instrument at the time, and ESA describes them as the most detailed ever taken of this galaxy.

The picture blends several kinds of light into one multi-wavelength image. Visible light shows the familiar structure of stars and dust. Ultraviolet light, invisible to our eyes, traces young stars. Near-infrared light slips through some of the dust, revealing detail that would otherwise be hidden behind it.

By combining these wavelengths, astronomers could see features in the dusty part of the galaxy that had never been seen before. Dust lanes like these block visible light, so looking at them in other wavelengths is one of the best ways to discover what lies inside.
explore: Centaurus A lies about 11 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus. The dust lanes that make it so recognisable are the focus of this close-up.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, so this image shows detail no human observer could see directly, even through a telescope.

alt: A close-up of a galaxy crossed by dark lanes of dust.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 2744, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Abell 2744, a massive cluster of galaxies nicknamed Pandora's Cluster. It was the first image to come from Hubble's Frontier Fields programme.

Astronomers think the cluster has had a very violent past, forming when several galaxy clusters piled into one another. But the Frontier Fields programme is interested in more than the cluster itself. It uses the enormous mass of such clusters as natural magnifying glasses.

This effect is called gravitational lensing. The gravity of a huge cluster bends the light of more distant galaxies behind it, magnifying and distorting them. By studying these lensing effects, Hubble can see farther into the distant Universe than it otherwise could. Abell 2744 was the first of six clusters to be targeted, in a three-year programme of 840 orbits that was expected to produce the deepest views of the Universe yet.
explore: Lensed background galaxies often appear stretched into arcs or smears, because the cluster's gravity distorts their light as well as magnifying it. Abell 2744 is the first Frontier Fields cluster to be shown in this way.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light in this image is invisible to the eye, and the distant galaxies are far too faint to see without long exposures from a telescope.

alt: A crowded field of galaxies from a massive galaxy cluster.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 253, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: The nearby spiral galaxy NGC 253 is shown here in sharp detail by the VLT Survey Telescope, the VST. ESO describes this portrait as probably the best wide-field view ever taken of the galaxy and its surroundings.

Regions of active star formation glow throughout NGC 253. The galaxy is producing new stars at a furious rate, which is why it is classed as a starburst galaxy. In such galaxies, gas is being turned into stars far faster than in a calmer spiral.

The image also served as a demonstration. The VST was then the newest telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory, and its job is to survey wide areas of sky. This view shows that it can take in a broad field while still delivering impressive image quality, the kind of combination survey astronomers need.
explore: NGC 253 lies about 11 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor. The data were processed with the VST-Tube system, developed by A. Grado and colleagues at the INAF-Capodimonte Observatory.

understand.summary: This image comes from the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of this data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect, and a large telescope collects far more light than the eye can.

alt: A spiral galaxy with luminous star-forming regions spread through its disc.

caption: The Antennae galaxies, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the Antennae galaxies, a pair of galaxies caught in the middle of merging. ESA describes it as the sharpest image yet of this colliding pair.

As the two galaxies smash into each other, the collision is triggering the birth of billions of stars. Most of them form in groups and clusters rather than on their own. The brightest and most compact of these groups are known as super star clusters.

Collisions between galaxies are rarely about individual stars crashing into one another, since the space between stars is vast. Instead, the huge clouds of gas in each galaxy are squeezed and compressed as they meet, and that compression can set off bursts of star formation. The Antennae show this process in action, which makes them a natural target for studying how such mergers build new stars.
explore: The Antennae lie about 75 million light-years away in the constellation Corvus. The brightest and most compact of the star groups born in their collision are the super star clusters, and this sharp Hubble view helps pick them out.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters, plus a filter that isolates glowing hydrogen. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of this image uses near-infrared light, which is invisible to the eye, and the galaxies are far too faint to see in this detail without a large telescope.

alt: Two merging galaxies seen by Hubble.

caption: The Needle Galaxy, NGC 4565, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: A spiral galaxy seen edge-on stretches across this image from ESO's Very Large Telescope, a bright yellowish bulge rising from its centre above prominent lanes of dust. This is NGC 4565, known for obvious reasons as the Needle Galaxy.
Sir William Herschel, who also discovered Uranus, first spotted it in 1785. It is one of the most famous examples of an edge-on spiral and sits in Coma Berenices, some 30 million light-years from us.

Seeing a spiral from the side hides its arms but shows off its thin disc and the dust within it. NGC 4565 is relatively close, only 12 times farther than the Andromeda galaxy, and relatively large, roughly a third larger than the Milky Way. That combination means it does not quite fit inside the field of view of the FORS instrument used for this picture.
explore: Many more distant galaxies are scattered across the background of this FORS image. They show why galaxies were once nicknamed island universes, meaning separate systems of stars floating in space. NGC 4565 itself spills past the frame.

understand.summary: This image comes from the FORS instrument on the Very Large Telescope and combines B, V, R and I filters, spanning visible to near-infrared light. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail by eye. A large telescope collects far more light, and part of the data is near-infrared light the eye cannot detect.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy stretched like a needle across the frame, with a yellowish central bulge and dark dust lanes, and background galaxies around it.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2500, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Wispy spiral arms swirl out from a bright, elongated core in this Hubble image of NGC 2500. The galaxy is a barred spiral, and it sits roughly 30 million light-years from us, in the northern constellation Lynx. William Herschel discovered it more than 200 years ago.

Bars like this one are more common than astronomers once believed. Around two-thirds of all spiral galaxies have a straight bar cutting through the middle, the Milky Way among them. Bars are glowing nurseries for new stars and help channel material toward a galaxy's active core.

NGC 2500 is still forming stars, but unevenly. Its upper half, where the arms are a little better defined, holds far more star-forming regions than the lower half, and they show up as bright, dotted islands of light.
explore: NGC 2500 also resembles our galaxy in its surroundings. The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, a gathering of over 50 galaxies loosely bound by gravity. NGC 2500 is part of a similar group, the NGC 2841 group, whose members include NGC 2541, NGC 2537, NGC 2552 and a bright spiral resembling Andromeda, NGC 2481.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail without a large telescope.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with wispy arms swirling from a bright, elongated core, dotted with bright islands of light, mostly in its upper half.

caption: The merging galaxy NGC 6240, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A tangle of gas, dust and stars spreads out in branching wisps, loops and tails, with a knotted, pinky-red region at its centre. This is NGC 6240, 400 million light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus. Its shape has been compared to a butterfly and, less flatteringly, to a lobster.

The galaxy did not start out like this. Its twisted form is the result of two galaxies drifting too close and merging. That collision set off bursts of star formation, and many of the hot young stars it produced have since exploded as supernovae. One, named SN 2013dc, was discovered in 2013. It does not appear in this image, though its position is marked.

At the heart of the jumble, the two galaxies' central supermassive black holes are spiralling toward each other. They are only some 3000 light-years apart, very close for a galaxy that spans 300 000 light-years, and are expected to merge into a single immense black hole.
explore: Hubble released an earlier image of NGC 6240 in 2008. The knotted central region seen here in pinky-red was only revealed by these newer observations from Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

understand.summary: This image combines visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too distant and faint to see like this by eye, and part of the data comes from near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

alt: An irregular, tangled galaxy with branching wisps, loops and tails of gas, dust and stars and a knotted pinky-red centre.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4710, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 4710, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on. At its centre is a faint, ghostly X-shaped structure.

Astronomers call a feature like this a boxy or peanut-shaped bulge. It comes from stars in the galaxy's bar moving up and down, out of the plane of the disc, and it is only visible when a galaxy is viewed edge-on. From other angles, the structure is not evident.

How the central bulges of spiral galaxies form and change is still an open question, and that puzzle is what drew astronomers to NGC 4710. The galaxy is also a bit of an oddity. Peanut-shaped bulges are often seen in spirals with small bulges and loosely wound arms, but they are less common in galaxies like NGC 4710, whose arms wrap tightly around a more prominent bulge.
explore: NGC 4710 lies about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. The edge-on view hides its spiral arms but lets astronomers see the vertical shape of its centre.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The faint X-shape is subtle even in Hubble's image, and the galaxy is far too dim to see in this detail by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a faint X-shaped structure visible at its centre.

caption: The interacting galaxies NGC 3447, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A diffuse, patchy blue glow covers the right side of this Hubble image, while a smaller clump sits at the upper left. They are two interacting galaxies about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Leo. The larger one is known as NGC 3447, or NGC 3447B to avoid confusion, since NGC 3447 can also refer to the pair. The smaller is NGC 3447A.

The two galaxies sit so close that their mutual gravity is pulling them into strange, twisted shapes. Astronomers know they are interacting, but they are unsure what either galaxy looked like before the tearing began.

That uncertainty makes the pair hard to classify. NGC 3447A seems to show the remains of a central bar and some disrupted spiral arms, features of certain spiral galaxies. NGC 3447B is labelled by some as a former spiral and by others as an irregular galaxy. With so many objects in the sky, keeping names and categories consistent is a challenge, and ambiguous cases like this one show why.
explore: Astronomers have been discovering and naming galaxies, stars and clouds for hundreds of years, and ESA notes that bringing all those conventions into one consistent system is very difficult. NGC 3447 is one example.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines visible and near-infrared filters with a very broad filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: These galaxies are far too faint to see like this by eye, and part of the data lies outside the range of light the eye can detect.

alt: A diffuse, patchy blue galaxy filling the right side of the frame, with a smaller clump at upper left.

caption: The radio galaxy Hercules A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Very Large Array
story: In the centre of this image sits a yellowish elliptical galaxy that looks quite ordinary in Hubble's visible-light view. Enormous jets spread out from it, visible only in radio data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array in New Mexico. The galaxy is Hercules A, some two billion light-years away.

It is anything but ordinary. The galaxy is roughly a thousand times more massive than the Milky Way and holds a central black hole of about 2.5 billion solar masses. It is also the brightest radio source in the constellation Hercules and one of the brightest outside our galaxy anywhere in the sky.

The jets are beams of very-high-energy plasma, subatomic particles and magnetic fields, fired at nearly the speed of light from near the black hole. They stretch one-and-a-half million light-years, dwarfing the galaxy. Ring-like structures in their outer parts suggest the black hole has erupted several times.
explore: The jets' innermost parts cannot be seen because their material moves so fast that its light is beamed away from us. A very hot, X-ray-emitting cloud of gas also surrounds the source but does not appear here. Hubble also shows a companion elliptical galaxy close to the centre that may be merging with Hercules A.

understand.summary: This is a composite of visible light from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and radio data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. The colour mapping for each data set is not published.
understand.eye: Radio waves are invisible to the eye, so the jets that dominate this image could never be seen directly, even through a telescope.

alt: A yellowish elliptical galaxy at the centre of the frame with enormous jets extending from it, among other galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 269-G57, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: A symmetrical spiral galaxy fills this image from ESO's Very Large Telescope. At its centre is an inner ring built from several closely coiled spiral arms, and around it two outer arms that seem to split into several branches. This is ESO 269-G57, located about 155 million light-years away toward the southern constellation Centaurus.

Many blue, diffuse patches dot the arms, and most of them are regions where stars are forming. The galaxy covers about 4 arc minutes of sky, which works out to nearly 200,000 light-years across, and it belongs to a well-known cluster of galaxies in this part of the sky.
Around it, faint and distant galaxies crowd the background, looking, as ESO puts it, like a large fleet of spaceships. Each one is a galaxy in its own right, much farther away than ESO 269-G57.
explore: The data were taken with the VLT's ANTU telescope and the FORS1 instrument during a single morning session, adding up to just over an hour of exposure. They were later drawn from the ESO Science Archive and processed by Henri Boffin.

understand.summary: This image comes from the FORS1 instrument on the Very Large Telescope and combines blue, visual and red filters, plus a hydrogen-alpha filter according to the caption. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see by eye. An exposure of over an hour with a large telescope was needed to capture its arms and the background galaxies.

alt: A symmetrical spiral galaxy with an inner ring of tightly wound arms and two branching outer arms dotted with blue patches, among faint background galaxies.

caption: The dwarf spiral galaxy NGC 6503, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Pink puffs dot the swirling arms of NGC 6503 in this Hubble image, marking places where new stars have recently formed. The galaxy is like a smaller version of the Milky Way, and it sits near a vast, nearly empty region of space.

Although its structure resembles our galaxy's, NGC 6503's disc spans just 30 000 light-years, about a third of the Milky Way's size, so astronomers classify it as a dwarf spiral. It lies roughly 17 million light-years away in the constellation Draco, and Arthur Auwers discovered it in July 1854.

The galaxy is perched at the edge of the Local Void, a giant hollow in space bordered by the Hercules and Coma galaxy clusters and by our own Local Group. Estimates of the void's size vary widely, from 30 million light-years across to over 150 million, so NGC 6503 has very little galactic company nearby.
explore: Its isolation led stargazer Stephen James O'Meara to give it a nickname, the Lost-In-Space Galaxy, in his book Hidden Treasures.
The unusual colour balance comes from unusual filters, with 28 minutes through a filter that passes only hydrogen emission and 12 minutes in near-infrared light.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Red shows light from glowing hydrogen gas in star-forming regions, and blue shows near-infrared light, coloured that way for contrast.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the pink and blue colouring here comes from the chosen filters rather than the galaxy's natural appearance.

alt: A spiral galaxy with swirling arms dotted with pink puffs of star formation.

caption: Stephan's Quintet, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble close-up shows the central part of Stephan's Quintet, a group of galaxies caught up in a gigantic collision. Strangely distorted shapes, lanes of dust crossing from one galaxy to another, and long streams of stars and gas stretching far from the centre all point to violent encounters.

The quintet is the prototype of a class called compact groups of galaxies, and astronomers have studied it intensively for decades. The pull of gravity between the galaxies, known as tidal interaction, has bent them out of shape and drawn them together. ESA describes the area as one of the most exciting star-forming regions in the local Universe.
Stephan's Quintet is also popular with amateur astronomers, who know it as a tough target even for good hobby telescopes. Hubble's view reveals the tangled detail that small telescopes cannot show.
explore: The image was built from archival Hubble observations, a mosaic of two WFPC2 pointings made in December 1998 and again in the middle of the following year. The group lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Pegasus.

understand.summary: This is a natural-colour composite from Hubble's WFPC2 camera. Red shows light through a filter at 814 nm, green through a filter at 569 nm, and blue through a filter at 450 nm.
understand.eye: Because it uses red, green and blue filters, this image approximates natural colour, but the galaxies are far too faint to see in such detail by eye.

alt: Several distorted galaxies close together, linked by dust lanes and long streams of stars and gas.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1433, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A bright white core sits at the centre of this galaxy, ringed by swirling structures like water circling a drain. Wispy rings of dust surround dark, hollow bubbles, and the outer rings are dotted with navy blue, pinkish, reddish and white points. This is NGC 1433, a nearby barred spiral, seen by Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI.

In mid-infrared light the galaxy looks completely different from optical views. Areas that appeared dark now glow, because clumps of dust and gas absorb light from forming stars and re-emit it as infrared. The arms show young stars releasing energy and, in places, blowing out the surrounding gas and dust.
At the centre, Webb's sharp view reveals a double ring. The ring is actually formed by closely wound spiral arms curling into an oval shape that follows the galaxy's bar.
explore: NGC 1433 is one of 19 galaxies targeted by the PHANGS collaboration. It is classed as a Seyfert, a galaxy fairly close to Earth whose core is bright and active. According to ESA, how bright the MIRI view is, and how little dust it shows, could hint at a recent merger or collision with another galaxy.

understand.summary: This image comes from Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument. Blue shows light at 7.7 microns, green at 10 and 11.3 microns, and red at 21 microns.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is completely invisible to the eye, so this is a view no human observer could have directly.

alt: A galaxy with a bright white core, swirling rings of dust around dark bubbles, and outer rings dotted with navy blue, pinkish, reddish and white points.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 3501, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A thin, glowing streak slices across this Hubble image, with only a few foreground stars and distant background galaxies for company. It is NGC 3501, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on, which gives it a long, very narrow look.

It is not as lonely as it appears. Just out of frame is its companion, NGC 3507, and the two travel through space together as a pair. They look very different from each other, which again comes down to perspective, since NGC 3507 is seen face-on, showing off its barred, swirling arms.

NGC 3501 is also a spiral, though a different kind from its partner. It has no bar through its centre. Instead, its loosely wound arms all start from the middle. Seen from the side, those arms appear as bright gas and stars glowing along the streak, mottled by dark lanes of dust that run across the galaxy.
explore: Contestant Nick Rose submitted a version of this picture to Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition. The finished picture shows how much detail the galaxy's thin edge still holds.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect.

alt: A thin, glowing edge-on galaxy slicing across a dark field with a few stars and small background galaxies.

caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 4866, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: An almost edge-on galaxy with a bright central bulge and faint lanes of dust stretches across this Hubble image, surrounded by a crowd of spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies. It is NGC 4866, a lenticular galaxy about 80 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

Lenticular galaxies fall somewhere between spirals and ellipticals in shape and character. NGC 4866's bulge is made mostly of old stars, and it shows no spiral arms. Because we see it nearly side-on, its disc stands out clearly, and a disc is something elliptical galaxies do not have.

Just to the right of the galaxy shines a very bright star that appears to sit inside NGC 4866's halo. It does not. The star is much closer to us, sitting between us and the galaxy, so the two merely line up from our viewpoint. Tricks of perspective like this are common and can mislead astronomers about where objects really are.
explore: Virgo is the largest constellation of the Zodiac and the second largest of all, after Hydra, but it is best known for how many galaxies lie within it. A version of this image was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Gilles Chapdelaine.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines a blue visible filter with a near-infrared filter. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot detect.

alt: An almost edge-on galaxy with a bright central bulge and faint dust lanes, a very bright star to its right, and many small galaxies in the background.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1187, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This portrait from ESO's Very Large Telescope shows NGC 1187, an impressive spiral galaxy about 60 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus, the River.

Spiral galaxies are flat, rotating discs of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind out from a central bulge. The arms are usually where new stars are forming, while older stars tend to gather toward the centre. From far away, the light of vast numbers of stars blends into the glow of the disc.

NGC 1187 has also seen violent events. Over the past thirty years, it has hosted two supernova explosions, the most recent in 2007. A supernova is the violent death of a star, and for a short time it can shine brightly enough to stand out against the combined light of its whole galaxy. Recording such events helps astronomers learn how often stars end their lives this way.
explore: The image was taken with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT using blue, visual and red filters. With two supernovae recorded in the last thirty years, NGC 1187 has proved to be a galaxy worth keeping an eye on.

understand.summary: This image comes from the FORS1 instrument on the Very Large Telescope and combines blue, visual and red filters in visible light. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see like this by eye, and a large telescope and long exposures are needed to reveal its structure.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen by the Very Large Telescope.

caption: The starburst galaxy NGC 5253, imaged by the Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This colour-coded composite shows NGC 5253, a small starburst galaxy at a distance of 11 million light-years. It combines three separate images from two different telescopes into one view.

The red channel comes from ESO's Very Large Telescope, which observed the galaxy in near-infrared light in the K-band, at a wavelength of 2.16 μm. The blue and green channels come from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope, which recorded two images in visible light. Combining ground- and space-based data like this lets astronomers bring together the strengths of each instrument.

A starburst galaxy is one that is forming stars at a much higher rate than usual. Infrared light is especially useful for studying such places, because it can pass through dust that blocks visible light and can reveal young stars and clusters hidden inside. The image covers a patch of sky 80 by 80 arcseconds, with north at the top and east to the left.
explore: NGC 5253 lies in the constellation Centaurus. The ESO release describes the region shown as home to a big stellar cluster within this blue dwarf galaxy.

understand.summary: This composite combines near-infrared data from the VLT's ISAAC instrument with visible-light data from Hubble. Red shows K-band infrared light at 2.16 μm, blue shows the V band at 0.55 μm, and green shows the I band at 0.79 μm.
understand.eye: The red channel is infrared light, invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a code for different wavelengths rather than what the galaxy would look like.

alt: A colour-coded image of a small galaxy, shown in red, green and blue.

caption: The blue compact dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In this Hubble image, an intense region of star formation sits inside the elliptical main body of the irregular galaxy NGC 5253, which appears red. At its heart, hot young stars gathered in clusters glow blue, and a faint, diffuse glow from ionised oxygen gas traces the starburst itself.

NGC 5253 is one of the nearest known Blue Compact Dwarf galaxies, about 12 million light-years away in Centaurus. Such galaxies form stars vigorously despite having little dust and relatively few elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, usually the raw ingredients of star birth.

Their molecular clouds are much like the untouched clouds from which the very first stars emerged in the young Universe, so astronomers see them as an ideal testbed for studying primordial star formation. NGC 5253 does hold some dust and heavier elements, but far less than the Milky Way.
explore: The galaxy belongs to the Centaurus A/Messier 83 group, and its peculiar nature may come from a close encounter with Messier 83. Blue compact dwarfs also connect to the Dwarf Galaxy Problem, in which simulations predict far more small satellite galaxies around big galaxies than are observed.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and infrared exposures. The caption says the main body appears red and the young star clusters blue, but the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Part of this image uses infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to view in such detail without Hubble.

alt: A reddish elliptical-shaped galaxy with a bright centre of blue star clusters and a faint diffuse glow.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1300, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A barred spiral galaxy faces us head-on in this Webb image. Its circular central region has a bright white point at the middle, ringed by light yellow. A prominent bar runs out from it and connects to orange spiral arms that turn counterclockwise, the whole shape forming a backward S. This is NGC 1300, 69 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus.

Webb observed the galaxy for the PHANGS programme, short for Physics at High Angular resolution in Nearby GalaxieS. It is a large project that combines observations of many galaxies from several telescopes in space and on the ground.

The aim is to study every stage of the star formation cycle. That runs from the birth of stars inside dusty clouds of gas to the energy those young stars release, which helps carve the intricate structures that Webb's infrared images reveal.
explore: This image is one of a large collection of Webb views of nearby galaxies released by the PHANGS team.

understand.summary: This image combines near-infrared data from Webb's NIRCam and mid-infrared data from MIRI. Blue shows light at 3.0 and 3.35 microns, green at 3.6 and 7.7 microns, and red at 7.7, 10, 11.3 and 21 microns.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are a translation of wavelengths the eye cannot detect.

alt: A face-on barred spiral galaxy with a bright white centre ringed by light yellow, a prominent bar and orange spiral arms forming a backward S shape.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1–2403, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.1–2403, one of six clusters studied by the Hubble Frontier Fields programme. As a set, those clusters have given astronomers their deepest ever views of gravitational lensing.

The cluster contains so much mass that it bends the light of objects lying behind it. In effect, it acts as a huge magnifying lens. Light from more distant galaxies passes close to the cluster, is deflected by its gravity, and arrives at Hubble brighter and larger than it would otherwise appear.

Astronomers have used this natural lens to look very far back in time. Using this cluster and two others, they found galaxies dating from a time when the Universe was only 600 to 900 million years old, counting from the Big Bang. Light from such galaxies has been travelling for most of the history of the Universe, so these objects show the Universe when it was young.
explore: The cluster lies in the direction of the constellation Eridanus. Lensed background galaxies often appear stretched or smeared, because the cluster's gravity distorts their light as well as magnifying it.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the distant lensed galaxies are far too faint to see without very long telescope exposures.

alt: A dense field of galaxies in a massive cluster, with many smaller, fainter galaxies scattered across a dark background.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACSJ0717.5+3745, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster MACSJ0717.5+3745, one of six studied by the Hubble Frontier Fields programme. Together, the six have yielded the deepest images of gravitational lensing ever made.

The cluster's enormous mass bends the light of objects behind it, turning the cluster into a natural magnifying lens. Light from distant galaxies is deflected as it passes through the cluster's gravity, making those galaxies look brighter and larger than they otherwise would.

MACSJ0717.5+3745 stands out even among the Frontier Fields. Few known galaxy clusters are as massive, and no known gravitational lens is larger. Of all the galaxy clusters astronomers have found and measured, this one lenses the largest area of the sky, which gives it an especially wide view of the distant galaxies beyond.
explore: The cluster lies in the direction of the constellation Auriga. Gravitational lensing can stretch the images of background galaxies into arcs as well as brighten them.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the lensed galaxies are far too faint to see without long exposures from a large telescope.

alt: A crowded field of galaxies belonging to a massive cluster, with fainter background galaxies scattered among them.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5468, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: We look straight down onto NGC 5468 in this Hubble image, seeing its loose, open spiral pattern in fine detail. The galaxy lies just over 130 million light-years away, in the constellation Virgo.

NGC 5468 is notable for its supernovae. In the last 20 years it has hosted several that astronomers observed, namely SN 1999cp, SN 2002cr, SN 2002ed, SN 2005P and SN 2018dfg. Because the galaxy faces us, it is easier to spot these new points of light as they appear.

Supernovae mainly happen in two ways. In one, a massive star runs out of fuel, can no longer support its own weight, collapses and explodes. In the other, a white dwarf in a pair of stars pulls more material from its companion than it can hold, sparking runaway nuclear fusion in its core. Either way, the explosion can briefly rival the light of an entire galaxy.
explore: The galaxy's supernovae include both of these types. The image acknowledges Judy Schmidt, known as Geckzilla, for her contribution.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of this image uses infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to view in this detail without a large telescope.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a loose, open spiral pattern.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4206, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Vast streaks of dust run along this edge-on spiral galaxy, partly veiling the bulge at its centre, which is only just visible. Near the edges, scattered clumps that appear blue mark places where new stars are being born. This is NGC 4206, about 70 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.
The bulge tells a different story from the edges. It is mostly made of older, redder stars, and very little star formation happens there.

Hubble took this image as part of a snapshot survey of nearby edge-on spirals. The goal was to measure how the material between stars, the interstellar medium, affects light passing through it. The Advanced Camera for Surveys can reveal the dust and hydrogen gas in the cold parts of that medium. Astronomers then map how the material absorbs and scatters light, an effect called extinction, which makes objects look redder to us.
explore: NGC 4206 shines at 13th magnitude and can be seen with most moderate amateur telescopes. William Herschel discovered it on 17 April 1784. Contestant Nick Rose submitted a version of this picture to Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The caption notes that star-forming clumps appear blue, but the filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy can be seen with moderate amateur telescopes, but not in this detail, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy crossed by vast streaks of dust that partly hide its central bulge, with blue clumps toward its edges.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 4517, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A spiral galaxy seen edge-on stretches across this Hubble image, crowned by a very bright star. The galaxy is NGC 4517, slightly larger than our Milky Way, and it lies about 40 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

The star is not part of the galaxy. It is much closer to us, which is why it looks so large and bright compared with the galaxy behind it. NGC 4517 does have a bright centre, but it is not visible in this Hubble view.

William Herschel discovered the galaxy in 1784. He described the scene as a fairly bright star sitting exactly north of the middle of a stretched-out milky ray. That milky ray was this galaxy, though his equipment could only show him a fuzzy, blurred shape below the much brighter star. Because of how it is oriented, NGC 4517 has featured in numerous studies of globular clusters, which are clumps of stars that orbit galaxy centres like satellites.
explore: A version was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Gilles Chapdelaine. ESA calls it another treasure unearthed from the Hubble archives.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Herschel saw only a fuzzy milky streak by eye through his telescope, while Hubble's near-infrared data and sharp resolution reveal far more.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy stretched across the frame with a very bright star above it.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1964, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: A bright, dense core sits inside a mottled oval disc, and around that disc curl distinct spiral arms speckled with bright starry regions. This is NGC 1964, a spiral galaxy roughly 70 million light-years away in the constellation Lepus, the Hare.

The galaxy shares its patch of sky with plenty of stars in our own Milky Way. The star HD 36785 sits just to the galaxy's right, with two more prominent stars, HD 36784 and TYC 5928-368-1, above it. The large, bright star below NGC 1964 is BD-22 1147. All of these are much closer to us than the galaxy.
William Herschel noticed the galaxy's brilliant centre on the night of 20 November 1784, which led to its discovery and its later entry in the New General Catalogue, the source of its NGC name.
explore: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla also picks up many background galaxies here. According to ESO, the instrument registers light from objects as much as 40 million times too faint for a human eye.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and combines blue and red visible-light filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy and the background galaxies are far too faint to see by eye. The instrument can record objects many millions of times fainter than the eye can detect.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a bright core inside a mottled oval disc and speckled arms, surrounded by several bright foreground stars and faint background galaxies.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy IC 4710, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A busy cloud of bright stars fills this Hubble image, with bright pockets scattered around its edges where bursts of new stars are forming. This is IC 4710, a dwarf irregular galaxy discovered in 1900 by astronomer DeLisle Stewart.

Irregular galaxies live up to their name. They look chaotic, with no central bulge and no spiral arms, setting them apart from spirals and ellipticals. Astronomers think some may once have been spirals or ellipticals that were pulled out of shape over time by the gravity of other galaxies during encounters or mergers.

Dwarf irregulars matter especially for understanding how galaxies change over cosmic time, because they are thought to resemble the very first galaxies that formed in the Universe. Studying nearby examples like IC 4710 gives a closer look at objects that may be similar to those early systems.
explore: The galaxy sits in Pavo, the Peacock, a southern constellation, roughly 25 million light-years from us. Pavo is also home to NGC 6752, ranked the third-brightest globular cluster in our sky, NGC 6744, a spiral galaxy, as well as six known planetary systems, including HD 181433, which hosts a super-Earth.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

alt: A loose, busy cloud of bright stars with brighter pockets scattered around its edges.

caption: The UFO Galaxy, NGC 2683, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Delicate lanes of dust are silhouetted against the golden haze of a galaxy's core, while clusters of young blue stars glitter through the disc. This is NGC 2683, a spiral seen almost edge-on. Its shape recalls a classic science-fiction spaceship, which is why astronomers at the Astronaut Memorial Planetarium and Observatory nicknamed it the UFO Galaxy.
A side-on view has its own advantages. It shows off the dusty lanes of the spiral arms, and the blue star clusters trace where new stars are forming.

Even from this angle, astronomers can work out a galaxy's structure. Studies of the properties of NGC 2683's light suggest it is a barred spiral, though the bar cannot be seen directly from our viewpoint. William Herschel discovered the galaxy on 5 February 1788. It lies in the northern constellation Lynx, named not for a resemblance to the cat but because it is faint enough to need a cat's sharp eyes.
explore: The image joins two neighbouring Hubble fields. A narrow, slightly blurred strip crossing most of the picture marks a gap between Hubble's detectors, patched with less detailed ground-based observations. The field is about 6.5 by 3.3 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and combines visible and near-infrared light, with a strip filled in from ground-based telescopes. The colour assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see in this detail by eye, and part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

alt: An almost edge-on spiral galaxy with dark dust lanes against a golden core and blue star clusters in its disc.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4639, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bar runs clearly through the bright, round core of NGC 4639 in this Hubble image, and the spiral arms are sprinkled with bright patches of star formation. The galaxy lies over 70 million light-years away in Virgo and is one of about 1500 galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.

Around two thirds of all spirals have a bar, and astronomers suspect they are a normal stage that spirals pass through as they develop. The bright patches in the arms look tiny, but each is several hundred light-years across and holds hundreds or thousands of newborn stars.

The core hides a massive black hole that is swallowing gas around it. This makes the centre an active galactic nucleus, or AGN, revealed by telltale features in the galaxy's light and by X-rays from hot gas falling inward. NGC 4639 is a very weak AGN, showing that such activity ranges widely, from quiet galaxies like this one to distant quasars.
explore: Most galaxies are thought to have a black hole at their centre. In quasars, the AGN's emission almost completely outshines the galaxy that hosts it. NGC 4639 sits at the quiet end of that range.

caption: The dwarf galaxy NGC 2366, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the dwarf galaxy NGC 2366 in detail. It has none of the elegant spiral arms seen in many larger galaxies, but it does hold a bright nebula where stars are forming.

The galaxy is also close enough that astronomers can make out its individual stars. That is valuable, because studying single stars in another galaxy lets researchers compare them directly with the stars of our own. In more distant galaxies, the light of countless stars blends together into a smooth glow.

Dwarf galaxies are much smaller than galaxies like the Milky Way, and many lack a tidy shape. A star-forming nebula is a cloud of gas lit up by hot young stars born inside it. In NGC 2366, that nebula stands out as a bright region among the galaxy's scattered stars.
explore: NGC 2366 lies about 10 million light-years away in the constellation Camelopardalis. ESA's entry for this image also lists the object NGC 2363.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 201, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble shows NGC 201 in fine detail, with a bright centre and barred spiral arms. The arms do not start directly at the core but seem offset, growing from a bar of stars that cuts through the middle. Like the Milky Way, it is a barred spiral. It lies 200 million light-years away in Cetus, the Sea Monster, and cannot be seen with the naked eye.

NGC 201 and three close neighbours outside the frame make up HCG 7, one of the Hickson Compact Groups. These are small, isolated gatherings of a few bright, compact galaxies close together. As they draw nearer, they interact strongly, pulling material into space and distorting one another.
Eventually, all the galaxies in such a group will merge. Simulations show that within a billion years they combine into one giant fossil galaxy, and this may be the final fate of all galaxy groups.
explore: William Herschel discovered NGC 201 in the late 1700s. A version of this image was submitted to Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Luca Limatola.

caption: The galaxy NGC 4861, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This galaxy looks rather like a comet, with a dense, luminous, colourful head and a dimmer tail trailing behind. It is NGC 4861, in the lesser-known constellation Canes Venatici, the Hunting Dogs.
Astronomers are still debating how to classify it. Its physical properties, such as mass, size and rotation speed, point to a spiral galaxy, but its appearance fits better with a dwarf irregular.

Small, messy galaxies like this are useful to study. Their gravity is weaker, so it takes less energy to move material around inside them. That makes them likely to be filled with galactic winds, fast streams of charged particles. Star formation can power such winds, and new stars are forming in NGC 4861's bright head, blasting out high-speed particles. It would seem an ideal place to study galactic winds, yet recent studies found none.
explore: NGC 4861 lies about 30 million light-years away, in Canes Venatici, a constellation home to a variety of deep-sky objects.

caption: The centre of the starburst galaxy M82, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A bright white core glows against the blackness of space, with dark brown tendrils of dust packed toward the centre. White points of many sizes are scattered across the scene, crowding most thickly near the middle. This is a section of M82, an edge-on starburst galaxy, seen in near-infrared light by Webb.

Found in Ursa Major, M82 is 12 million light-years from Earth. It is forming stars 10 times faster than the Milky Way. For a long time, curtains of dust and gas have hidden that process from view, but Webb's infrared vision can see through them.

With Webb's sharp resolution, astronomers can pick out small, bright, compact sources, each of which is either a single star or a star cluster. An accurate tally of them could reveal the separate stages of star birth and how long each stage takes.
explore: The NIRCam view shows the galaxy's centre in unprecedented detail. It comes from a survey of M82 by a team of astronomers using Webb. Webb's infrared view makes such a census possible.

understand.summary: This image comes from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera, NIRCam. Red shows light at 2.12 microns, green at 1.64 microns and blue at 1.40 microns.
understand.eye: All of this light is near-infrared and invisible to the eye. In visible light, the dust that Webb sees through would hide much of this detail.
